alternative_regimens.summary: May accompany hysterectomy after consideration of the consequences of early menopause and potential need for MHT.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider individually when choosing between ovarian conservation and removal.

not_recommended.name: sub-total hysterectomy
not_recommended.reason: Total hysterectomy is recommended instead because endometriosis can persist in or beside the retained cervix.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No RCTs of hysterectomy for endometriosis-associated pain were identified in the guideline; the potential recurrence risk with ovarian conservation must be weighed against the effects of oophorectomy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with a history of endometriosis who require MHT.
decision_rules: Use a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen when MHT is required.

recommended_regimens.name: continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommended form of MHT for women with previous endometriosis who need menopausal hormone therapy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic review restricted to two RCTs reported a small association between MHT and endometriosis recurrence.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes evidence on MHT following surgical menopause for endometriosis as scarce.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with endometriosis and infertility who are actively trying to conceive, whether or not they also have pain.
decision_rules: Do not prescribe hormonal suppression while the woman is trying to conceive because available hormonal treatments interfere with ovulation.
Assess disease stage or type and fertility factors, including ovarian reserve and semen analysis; involve the fertility team to tailor treatment.
When contemplating surgery, consider age, ovarian reserve, duration of infertility, other fertility factors, symptoms, prior operations and the woman's preferences.

not_recommended.name: hormonal suppression
not_recommended.reason: It should not be prescribed to women attempting conception; available hormonal endometriosis treatments interfere with ovulation. A Cochrane review found no benefit in clinical pregnancy rates from ovarian suppression versus placebo, while live-birth data were lacking.

supportive_care: Consider earlier referral for fertility assessment and treatment because endometriosis is a known infertility risk factor.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If conception cannot or will not be attempted immediately after surgery, ovarian suppression may be considered for pain management; the guideline states that postoperative hormone therapy does not negatively affect future fertility.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with stage I-II endometriosis and associated infertility.
decision_rules: Offer operative laparoscopy to improve the chance of ongoing clinical pregnancy.
Consider IUI with ovarian stimulation as another management option, particularly within six months after surgery when available.
Make surgical decisions jointly after considering pain, ovarian reserve, age, duration of infertility, previous surgery and other fertility investigations.

recommended_regimens.name: operative laparoscopy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for infertility associated with stage I-II endometriosis.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A 2020 Cochrane review found improved chances of viable intrauterine pregnancy after surgery compared with diagnostic laparoscopy alone; live-birth data were lacking.

recommended_regimens.name: IUI with ovarian stimulation
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider for infertility with stage I-II endometriosis.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline cites RCT evidence of higher live-birth rates with stimulated IUI than with expectant management and higher biochemical pregnancy rates than with IUI alone.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: May be particularly effective within six months of surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence of improvement in live birth following operative laparoscopy is lacking.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with an endometrioma and associated infertility who are seeking spontaneous pregnancy.
decision_rules: Clinicians may consider operative laparoscopy because it may improve spontaneous pregnancy chances.
Decide with the woman after assessing ovarian reserve, previous surgery, symptoms, other fertility investigation results and plans for fertility treatment.
Exercise particular caution with recurrent or bilateral endometriomas because surgery can adversely affect ovarian reserve.

recommended_regimens.name: operative laparoscopy
recommended_regimens.summary: May be considered for endometrioma-associated infertility when seeking spontaneous conception.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a study by Candiani et al., postoperative pregnancy rates after cystectomy and CO2 laser cyst vaporisation were 72.2% and 74.3%, respectively; spontaneous pregnancy rates were 55.5% vs 35.9%, respectively.

alternative_regimens.name: expectant management
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited narrative review suggested that observation of an asymptomatic endometrioma is reasonable, while noting concern about possible ovarian-reserve decline.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider individually for an asymptomatic endometrioma rather than treating a cited review's suggestion as a formal guideline recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: RCT evidence comparing surgery with conservative management for infertility in ovarian endometriosis is lacking.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with an endometrioma who are planning ART.
decision_rules: Do not routinely operate on the endometrioma before ART.
Surgery may be considered to address pain or improve access to follicles for oocyte retrieval.

alternative_regimens.name: surgery for endometrioma
alternative_regimens.summary: An option before ART for symptoms or follicle accessibility, not a routine prerequisite.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Pain management or difficulty accessing follicles.

not_recommended.name: routine surgery for endometrioma prior to ART
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against routine pre-ART surgery, while allowing consideration for pain or follicle access.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited meta-analysis found fewer oocytes retrieved in women with endometriomas but no other differences in reproductive outcomes with IVF or ICSI.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with deeply infiltrative endometriosis and infertility, particularly those with symptoms.
decision_rules: Consider operative laparoscopy as an option, guided by pain symptoms and the woman's preference.
When considering excision before ART, base the decision on pain and preference rather than assuming a proven reproductive benefit.

recommended_regimens.name: operative laparoscopy
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider as a surgical option for deeply infiltrative endometriosis with infertility, according to symptoms and the woman's wishes.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A review of 49 studies on surgery for deeply infiltrative endometriosis reported pregnancy rates of 23-57% and cumulative pregnancy rates of 58-70% within four years, but only 37% of studies reported pregnancy rates. Missing information and poor-quality data prevented firm conclusions about fertility benefit.

alternative_regimens.name: ART
alternative_regimens.summary: A fertility treatment option that does not automatically require prior excision of deeply infiltrative disease.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider according to fertility circumstances, pain symptoms and the woman's preference.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence that surgery for deeply infiltrative endometriosis improves reproductive outcomes is scarce; a cited systematic review found no randomised controlled trials of fertility outcomes after this surgery.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with stage III-IV endometriosis and infertility whose tubes are proven patent.
decision_rules: IUI with ovarian stimulation could be considered, but recognise that evidence for this stage is limited.

alternative_regimens.name: IUI with ovarian stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible infertility treatment when tubal patency is established; evidence in stage III-IV disease is limited to retrospective data.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Stage III-IV endometriosis with proven patent tubes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes retrospective evidence suggesting an increased ongoing pregnancy rate with six cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation; it does not extend its graded stage I-II IUI recommendation to stage III-IV disease.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with infertility associated with endometriosis, particularly impaired tubal function or co-existing male factor infertility.
decision_rules: Use ART to treat endometriosis-associated infertility, especially with tubal impairment or a co-existing male fertility factor.
Consider whether surgery before ART is needed for tubal disease, deeply infiltrative endometriosis or ovaries inaccessible for oocyte retrieval.
Consider EFI when estimating chances of spontaneous or IUI conception following surgery and identifying women who may benefit from ART.

recommended_regimens.name: ART
recommended_regimens.summary: Use to treat infertility associated with endometriosis; the guideline includes in vitro fertilisation and ICSI among these interventions.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Evidence on ART outcomes was conflicting. A cited systematic review found no significant overall difference in clinical pregnancy or live-birth rates between women with and without endometriosis, but found lower clinical pregnancy rates and a trend towards lower live-birth rates with stage III-IV disease. A separate USA retrospective cohort reported a 24% lower live-birth rate on the first treatment cycle in women with endometriosis than in women with unexplained infertility.

supportive_care: Assess ovarian reserve and semen analysis as part of individualised fertility planning, with fertility-team involvement.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline found no randomised controlled trials comparing ART with expectant management in women with endometriosis. A cited review found moderate-quality evidence that salpingectomy before ART for tubal disease probably increases pregnancy rates; evidence that tubal occlusion may increase pregnancy rates was low quality.

special_populations.population: Women with endometriosis-associated infertility who are trying to conceive
special_populations.considerations: Pain management may be difficult because hormonal treatments used for endometriosis suppress ovulation. Assessment should account for age, ovarian reserve, duration of infertility, previous surgery, other fertility factors and the partner’s semen analysis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not prescribe hormonal suppression while the woman is trying to conceive. Offer operative laparoscopy for stage I-II endometriosis with infertility; consider IUI with ovarian stimulation. ART can be used, particularly when tubal function is impaired or male factor infertility coexists.

special_populations.population: Women with endometriosis who are not ready to attempt conception immediately after surgery
special_populations.considerations: Postoperative hormonal treatment may improve pain without adversely affecting future fertility.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Hormonal suppression may be considered after surgery if there are no immediate plans to conceive.

special_populations.population: Women with ovarian endometrioma and infertility considering ART
special_populations.considerations: The presence of an endometrioma may impede access to follicles. Surgery also carries a risk of reducing ovarian reserve.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not routinely operate on an endometrioma before ART; surgery may be considered for pain or to enable access to follicles.

special_populations.population: Women with recurrent or bilateral endometrioma
special_populations.considerations: Cystectomy requires particular caution because of its potential effect on ovarian reserve. Before surgery for bilateral endometriomas, the possibility of freezing oocytes should be discussed.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Carefully assess whether to operate and minimise ovarian damage if surgery proceeds.

special_populations.population: Women with deeply infiltrative endometriosis involving the bowel, bladder or ureter
special_populations.considerations: Disease affecting these organs may impair their function and requires specialist assessment. Decisions about surgery should include discussion of expected benefits and risks.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Refer to a specialist endometriosis service. Surgical removal should be undertaken by a surgeon experienced in deep disease, preferably within a multidisciplinary setting using a minimally invasive approach aimed at removing all lesions.

special_populations.population: Women with a history of endometriosis who require menopausal hormone therapy
special_populations.considerations: If oophorectomy is contemplated, discuss the consequences of early menopause and the possible need for menopausal hormone therapy (MHT).
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen if MHT is required.

special_populations.population: Women with endometriosis who have no symptoms
special_populations.considerations: Endometriosis may be found incidentally during laparoscopy performed for another reason.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treatment does not need to be started solely because endometriosis is present without symptoms.

special_populations.population: People whose gender identity does not align with the sex assigned at birth
special_populations.considerations: Although the guideline generally uses the terms ‘woman’ and ‘women’s health’, care should be inclusive, sensitive and individualised, including use of each person’s preferred gender nouns and pronouns.

special_populations.population: Women with previous or current trauma accessing maternity care
special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy, birth, postpartum care and examinations may trigger trauma, whether or not a history has been disclosed. Staff should communicate clearly, obtain consent before procedures and provide care that preserves dignity and psychological safety.

artifacts.title: Key Recommendations

rows: Consider endometriosis when a woman has one or more of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—especially dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—especially dysuria and/or haematuria—or infertility.
Offer abdominal and pelvic examination when symptoms suggest endometriosis; assess for reduced organ mobility, tender posterior vaginal nodules, and pelvic or abdominal masses.
Do not postpone discussing and starting empirical treatment for suspected endometriosis; treatment may improve quality of life.

Refer suspected or confirmed endometriosis to a Gynaecologist when symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent; examination shows endometriosis; infertility is present; initial management fails, is intolerable or is contraindicated; or imaging suggests higher-stage or deeply infiltrating disease, such as an endometrioma or invasion of another organ.
Refer suspected or confirmed deeply infiltrative endometriosis affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter to a specialist endometriosis service.
Offer transvaginal ultrasound during assessment of suspected endometriosis; consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is inappropriate.
Do not use MRI as the initial diagnostic investigation for endometriosis; use it when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected.
Do not use computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) to diagnose endometriosis.
Negative imaging must not be used to rule out endometriosis.
Do not use biomarkers, including serum CA-125, to diagnose endometriosis.
Consider laparoscopy for symptoms suggestive of endometriosis when empirical treatment is unsuitable or ineffective, including when imaging is negative.
Biopsy lesions suspected of endometriosis during laparoscopy for histological confirmation; a negative histological result does not completely exclude the condition.
Refer to a Gynaecologist with suitable laparoscopic training and skills to optimise examination of the pelvis and abdomen at laparoscopy.
Offer analgesics, including paracetamol, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories and neuromodulator therapies, to reduce endometriosis-associated pain.
Offer combined hormonal contraception or progestogens as initial hormonal treatment for endometriosis-associated pain.
Offer GnRH agonists or antagonists together with add-back hormone replacement therapy as second-line treatment for endometriosis-associated pain.
Make treatment decisions jointly with the woman, taking account of plans to conceive, adverse effects, cost and availability.
Consider hormonal suppression after endometriosis surgery if the woman does not intend to conceive immediately.
Offer surgery as an option for reducing endometriosis-associated pain.
Choose between hormonal and surgical pain treatment jointly with the woman, considering her preferences, adverse effects, individual effectiveness, costs and availability.
When operating for endometriosis-associated pain, clinicians may consider excision rather than ablation.
When operating on a painful endometrioma, anticipate other endometriosis lesions, including deeply infiltrative endometriosis, because these are commonly found.
For ovarian endometrioma, perform cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage and coagulation to reduce recurrence of the endometrioma and associated pain; minimise injury to the ovary.
Removal of deeply infiltrative endometriosis may lessen associated pain and improve quality of life.
An experienced deep-endometriosis surgeon should remove deeply infiltrative disease, preferably with a multidisciplinary team using a minimally invasive approach aimed at removing all lesions.
Consider hysterectomy, with or without oophorectomy, when conception is not planned and conservative treatment has failed; explain that symptoms do not invariably resolve.
Perform total rather than sub-total hysterectomy.
If oophorectomy is contemplated, discuss early-menopause consequences and the possible need for menopausal hormone therapy (MHT).
If a woman with previous endometriosis needs MHT, use a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen.
Do not prescribe hormonal suppression to women with endometriosis-associated infertility who are attempting conception.
Before surgery for endometriosis-related infertility, consider age, ovarian reserve, infertility duration and other fertility factors.
Offer operative laparoscopy for infertility associated with stage I-II endometriosis because it improves the prospect of an ongoing clinical pregnancy.

Operative laparoscopy may be considered for an endometrioma with infertility to improve the chance of spontaneous pregnancy; decide jointly after considering ovarian reserve, previous surgery, symptoms, other fertility-test findings and plans for fertility treatment.
Do not routinely operate on an endometrioma before assisted reproductive technology (ART); surgery may be considered for pain or to permit access to follicles.
Consider operative laparoscopy as an option for women with deeply infiltrative endometriosis and infertility, according to pain symptoms and the woman's preference.
Consider Intra-uterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation for infertility associated with stage I-II endometriosis.
Use ART for endometriosis-associated infertility, particularly with impaired tubal function or coexisting male-factor infertility.
Role of non-medical interventions for the treatment of endometriosis

No recommendation can be made for any individual non-medical intervention—traditional Chinese medicine, nutrition, electrotherapy, acupuncture, physiotherapy or psychological interventions—for endometriosis-related symptoms; clinicians may discuss them to address quality of life and psychological well-being.

rows: 1. OBJECTIVES: State the guideline's overall aims and anticipated health benefits.
Specify the health intent, expected outcomes and population or societal targets.
2. QUESTIONS: State the health questions underlying key recommendations.
Identify the population, interventions or exposures, comparators where relevant, outcomes and care setting.
3. POPULATION: Describe whom the guideline applies to.
Identify sex and age, relevant condition and disease severity or stage, comorbidities and excluded groups where applicable.
4. GROUP MEMBERSHIP: Identify everyone involved in guideline development.
Give participants’ names, disciplines, institutions, geographical locations and development-group roles.
5. TARGET POPULATION PREFERENCES AND VIEWS: Explain how target-population views were obtained and used.
Describe the strategy and methods for obtaining views, information gathered, and its influence on development or recommendations.
6. TARGET USERS: Identify the guideline's intended users.
Describe the intended audience and how the guideline may inform clinical decisions, policy or standards of care.
7. SEARCH METHODS: Describe the evidence-search strategy.
List databases or other sources, search periods and terms, and provide the complete strategy.
8. EVIDENCE SELECTION CRITERIA: Explain study inclusion and exclusion.
Describe relevant population characteristics, study design, comparisons, outcomes, language and context, with rationale where appropriate.
9. STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE: Assess individual studies and the evidence overall.
Address study designs and methods, outcome relevance, consistency and direction of findings, benefits versus harms and applicability.
10. FORMULATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS: Explain how recommendations and final decisions were reached.
Report the development process, resolution of disagreement and influence of that process on final recommendations.
11. CONSIDERATION OF BENEFITS AND HARMS: Explain how benefits and risks informed recommendations.
Provide supporting benefits and harms data, their balance, and the relationship of that balance to recommendations.
12. LINK BETWEEN RECOMMENDATIONS AND EVIDENCE: Make the evidentiary basis of recommendations explicit.
Describe how evidence informed each recommendation and link recommendations to key studies, summaries or tables.
13. EXTERNAL REVIEW: Describe the external-review process.
Give its purpose, methods, reviewers, findings and influence on the guideline or recommendations.
14. UPDATING PROCEDURE: Describe how the guideline will be revised.
State that updating will occur, its interval or triggers, and the method to be used.
15. SPECIFIC AND UNAMBIGUOUS RECOMMENDATIONS: Define appropriate actions by situation and population.
State the action and purpose, relevant population, qualifications and any uncertainty about the best option.
16. MANAGEMENT OPTIONS: Present the available approaches.
Describe management options and the clinical circumstances or populations suited to each.
17. IDENTIFIABLE KEY RECOMMENDATIONS: Make principal recommendations easy to locate.
Present them in a distinct summary, formatting or algorithm, or group them together.
18. FACILITATORS AND BARRIERS TO APPLICATION: Describe implementation factors.
Explain which factors were assessed, how they were identified, what emerged and how they influenced development.
19. IMPLEMENTATION ADVICE/TOOLS: Provide practical application support.
Identify summaries, checklists, algorithms, manuals, responses to barriers, facilitator tools and pilot-test findings where applicable.
20. RESOURCE IMPLICATIONS: Describe resources needed to apply recommendations.
Identify costs considered, how information was obtained, findings and their influence on guideline development.

Specify adherence and impact measures, measurement frequency and operational definitions.
22. FUNDING BODY: Disclose funding and its influence.
Name the funding source or state that there was none, and address whether it influenced content.
23. COMPETING INTERESTS: Disclose group members’ interests.
Describe interests assessed, how declarations were sought, interests identified and their influence on recommendations.
