document_sections.heading: Diagnosis of endometriosis
document_sections.content: Key recommendations: Consider endometriosis when a woman has at least one of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea that disrupts daily activities, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—especially dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—especially dysuria or haematuria—or infertility (Best practice). Offer abdominal and pelvic examination when symptoms suggest endometriosis; look for restricted organ mobility, tender posterior vaginal nodules and pelvic or abdominal masses (Grade 1C). Do not delay discussion or initiation of empirical treatment for suspected disease, since treatment may improve quality of life (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed cases to a Gynaecologist for severe, persistent or recurrent symptoms; examination findings; associated infertility; ineffective, intolerable or contraindicated initial management; or imaging suggestive of a higher stage or deeply infiltrating disease, including endometrioma or invasion of other organs (Best practice). Refer suspected or confirmed deeply infiltrative disease affecting the bowel, bladder or ureter to a specialist endometriosis service (Best practice). Offer transvaginal ultrasound during investigation and consider transabdominal ultrasound when the transvaginal approach is unsuitable (Grade 1A). MRI is not a first-line diagnostic investigation, but is recommended when deeply infiltrative disease of the bowel, bladder or ureter is suspected (Grade 1B). Do not use computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) to diagnose endometriosis (Best practice). Negative imaging must not be used to exclude endometriosis (Grade 1B). Do not use biomarkers, including serum CA-125, for diagnosis (Grade 1A). Consider laparoscopy for suggestive symptoms when empirical treatment fails or is unsuitable, including when imaging is negative (Best practice). Biopsy suspected lesions during laparoscopy for histological confirmation; negative histology does not completely exclude disease (Grade 1B). Refer for laparoscopy to a Gynaecologist with suitable laparoscopic training and skills to optimise assessment of the abdomen and pelvis (Best practice).

document_sections.heading: Treatment of endometriosis-associated pain
document_sections.content: Key recommendations: Offer analgesics, including paracetamol, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories and neuromodulator therapies, to reduce pain (Grade 2B). Offer combined hormonal contraception or progestogens as first-line hormonal treatment (Grade 1A), and GnRH agonists or antagonists with add-back hormone replacement therapy as second-line treatment (Best practice). Make treatment decisions jointly with the woman, considering pregnancy intentions, adverse effects, cost and availability (Best practice). Consider postoperative hormonal suppression unless conception is planned immediately (Grade 1A). Offer surgery as an option for pain reduction (Grade 1A). For hormonal or surgical treatment, use shared decision-making that considers preferences, adverse effects, individual effectiveness, cost and availability (Best practice). If operating, clinicians may favour excision over ablation for pain (Grade 2A). Anticipate other disease, including deeply infiltrative endometriosis, during surgery for a painful endometrioma (Best practice). For ovarian endometrioma, perform cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage and coagulation to reduce cyst and pain recurrence, while limiting ovarian injury (Grade 1B). Removal of deeply infiltrative disease may lessen pain and improve quality of life (Grade 1B); an experienced deep-disease surgeon should perform it, preferably with a multidisciplinary team, a minimally invasive approach and the aim of removing all lesions (Best practice). Consider hysterectomy with or without oophorectomy after unsuccessful conservative care in women not planning conception, while explaining that symptoms may persist (Grade 2B). Prefer total to sub-total hysterectomy (Best practice). If considering oophorectomy, discuss early menopause and possible menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) (Grade 1B). If MHT is needed after endometriosis, recommend a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen (Grade 1C).

document_sections.heading: Treatment of endometriosis-associated infertility
document_sections.content: Key recommendations: Do not prescribe hormonal suppression to women with endometriosis and infertility who are attempting conception (Grade 1A). When considering fertility surgery, account for age, ovarian reserve, infertility duration and other fertility factors (Best practice). Offer operative laparoscopy for infertility with stage I-II disease to improve the chance of ongoing clinical pregnancy (Grade 1A). Operative laparoscopy may be considered for infertility with endometrioma to improve the chance of spontaneous pregnancy; decide jointly after considering ovarian reserve, earlier surgery, symptoms, other fertility investigations and planned fertility treatment (Grade 1A). Do not routinely operate on endometrioma before assisted reproductive technology (ART), although pain or follicle accessibility may justify surgery (Best practice). Consider operative laparoscopy as an option for symptomatic deeply infiltrative disease with infertility, according to pain and the woman's preference (Grade 2B). Consider Intra-uterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation for infertility with stage I-II disease (Grade 2B). Use ART for endometriosis-associated infertility, particularly with impaired tubal function or coexisting male-factor infertility (Grade 1C).

document_sections.heading: Role of non-medical interventions for the treatment of endometriosis
document_sections.content: Key recommendation: Evidence does not permit recommendations for any individual traditional Chinese medicine, nutritional, electrotherapy, acupuncture, physiotherapy or psychological intervention to relieve endometriosis-related symptoms. Clinicians may nevertheless discuss these approaches to support quality of life and psychological well-being (Best practice).

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Purpose
document_sections.content: The guideline aims to provide comprehensive, evidence-based direction within Irish healthcare for assessing and managing women with suspected or confirmed endometriosis, including its effects on quality of life and fertility.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Scope Target Users
document_sections.content: The intended users are healthcare professionals caring for people with possible or established endometriosis in general practice, general or specialist gynaecology, nursing, midwifery, imaging, allied health and social care. Management of adenomysosis and unspecified chronic pelvic pain falls outside its scope. Its target population comprises all women undergoing endometriosis assessment or management.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Objective To provide evidence-based recommendations for the assessment and management of endometriosis.
document_sections.content: The objectives are evidence-based assessment and management recommendations and a nationally consistent approach across primary, gynaecological and tertiary care, with particular attention to quality of life and fertility.

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Disclaimer
document_sections.content: The guideline supports consistent multidisciplinary practice but does not replace clinical judgement tailored to an individual woman's findings, available options, local expertise and resources. Clinicians remain responsible for confidential and respectful discussion, interpreters when necessary, explaining choices and obtaining informed consent, practising within professional and legal requirements, using appropriate precautions and documenting care.

document_sections.heading: 1.8 Use of language
document_sections.content: Although the guideline uses 'woman' and 'women’s health', these terms do not encompass everyone who might use reproductive healthcare. Services should be inclusive and sensitive to people whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth. Care should affirm sexual and gender identities, recognise different routes to pregnancy and use each person's preferred gender nouns and pronouns. Clear, respectful language supports informed decisions.

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Adopting a trauma-informed approach to maternity care
document_sections.content: Past or current trauma can be triggered during pregnancy, birth or postpartum care, including by procedures clinicians regard as routine, abdominal palpation, breastfeeding support and vaginal examination. Trauma-informed care seeks psychological safety and prevention of re-traumatisation. Its 4Rs are realisation, recognition and response to trauma, and resistance to re-traumatisation. Staff should recognise possible trauma even when it has not been disclosed, communicate clearly, obtain consent before interventions and preserve dignity and respect. A universally agreed approach has not yet been established; implementation requires organisational commitment, investment and change.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-mediated inflammatory disorder of uncertain cause, defined by endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus. Deposits commonly affect pelvic structures including ovaries, fallopian tubes, peritoneum and uterosacral ligaments. Deeply infiltrative endometriosis (DIE) may affect bowel, bladder or ureter and impair organ function; disease can also occur outside the pelvis, involve nerve roots or be found incidentally during laparoscopy in an asymptomatic person. It mainly affects reproductive-age women, although symptoms can begin in youth or persist after menopause. Estimated prevalence is 1 in 10 women; the World Health Organization estimates 190 million affected women worldwide. Anatomical severity and symptom severity need not correspond. Symptoms are not specific and overlap with bowel, bladder, musculoskeletal and fibromyalgia-related conditions. Absent specific biomarkers, limited imaging sensitivity for peritoneal disease, limited awareness and normalisation of symptoms contribute to missed or delayed diagnosis. Pain may disrupt activities, employment, physical and mental well-being, relationships, sexual function and fertility. The reported average interval from symptom onset to confirmed diagnosis is 7-8 years. Persistent symptoms during that interval may impair quality of life, undermine the patient–physician relationship and contribute to central sensitisation. A multicentre study in Europe, the UK and USA estimated annual costs of €9579 per affected woman, predominantly from work absence. Treatment addresses pain with analgesia, medical disease suppression and/or surgery; infertility requires separate consideration.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: The guideline supports Ireland's National Framework for Endometriosis Care, launched in March 2023. It addresses clinical diagnosis, imaging for diagnosis and surgical planning, medical and surgical treatment, infertility, service needs, and future audit and research. Its evidence base draws on the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) Endometriosis Guideline 2022, NICE Clinical Guideline (NG 73) 2017 and the Royal Australia and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) guideline 2021, together with subsequently published relevant studies. A central aim is earlier recognition of suggestive symptoms and signs so that clinicians can initiate treatment and consider appropriate investigations.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.1: What should the clinical assessment of a woman with suspected endometriosis include?
document_sections.content: Clinical assessment must include at least a history and physical examination.

document_sections.heading: History
document_sections.content: Common presentations include activity-limiting dysmenorrhoea, chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia during or after intercourse, cyclical gastrointestinal symptoms—particularly dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms and infertility accompanied by one or more other symptoms. A retrospective UK general-practice analysis reported associations with abdominopelvic pain (odds ratio (OR) = 5.2), dysmenorrhea (OR = 8.1), infertility (OR = 8.2) and dyspareunia (OR = 6.8). In a prospective multicentre study (n=1396), a symptoms-only model for Stage 3 and Stage 4 disease at first laparoscopy had sensitivity 82.3% and specificity 75.8%; combining symptoms with ultrasound improved prediction. A table adapted from Chapron et al. presents symptom-specific odds ratios and illustrates the predictive importance of cyclical symptoms. Other possible manifestations include fatigue (50-87% of women with endometriosis), cyclical cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, pneumothorax, shoulder-tip pain and scar swelling. Multiple symptoms, especially combined with clinical signs, increase diagnostic likelihood. Patient-reported information collected through technological tools may help predict disease and facilitate earlier diagnosis and referral.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Examination
document_sections.content: Offer examination, including pelvic examination when appropriate, to seek findings such as restricted organ mobility. A retrospective study of almost 800 infertile women with surgically confirmed disease identified poor uterine mobility as predictive. Vaginal examination can identify deep infiltration or nodules in the vagina, uterosacral ligaments or pouch of Douglas; speculum examination can show vaginal lesions. Rectovaginal examination may detect rectosigmoid infiltration, masses or adnexal masses/endometriomas. Significant findings can prompt earlier referral. ESHRE and NICE 2017 judged evidence for diagnostic accuracy of examination to be low: examination alone is unreliable, subtle signs may be missed and a normal examination does not exclude disease.

document_sections.heading: Early treatment and referral
document_sections.content: When symptoms and signs suggest endometriosis, discuss and offer empirical medical treatment without awaiting imaging, surgery or histology; earlier pain management may improve quality of life. Pregnancy has not been shown to cure endometriosis, so it should not be advised as symptom treatment.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: History and examination can support a working diagnosis and timely treatment before confirmatory investigations. Consider endometriosis with chronic pelvic pain, activity-limiting dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms—particularly dyschezia—cyclical urinary symptoms—particularly dysuria or haematuria—or infertility. Fatigue, cyclical cough, haemoptysis, chest pain, pneumothorax, shoulder-tip pain and scar swelling are additional possible manifestations; several symptoms, particularly cyclical ones, increase suspicion. Offer abdominal palpation and appropriate vaginal examination. Bimanual examination may identify restricted uterine mobility, endometriomas or deep nodules; appropriate speculum examination may reveal vaginal lesions. Consider rectovaginal examination for rectosigmoid disease only with explicit consent and awareness of discomfort. Discuss empirical treatment when history and examination suggest disease. Refer to a gynaecologist for ineffective, intolerable or contraindicated empirical treatment—including when conception is being attempted—examination findings, or severe, persistent or recurrent symptoms. Suspected deep involvement of bowel, bladder or ureters warrants specialist endometriosis referral.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.2: How reliable are imaging technologies for diagnosing endometriosis?
document_sections.content: The long diagnostic delay substantially burdens affected women. Laparoscopy has commonly served as the diagnostic gold standard but is invasive and entails potential morbidity and mortality. An inexpensive, sensitive and specific non-invasive diagnostic approach is identified as a research priority.

document_sections.heading: ULTRASOUND IMAGING Evidence Statement
document_sections.content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is widely accessible, relatively inexpensive and generally tolerated. It is useful for ovarian endometrioma and may detect deeply infiltrative bowel, bladder or ureteric disease. In Nisenblat et al.'s review of 49 studies involving 4807 women and using surgical diagnosis as comparator, TVUS for superficial pelvic disease had 95% specificity and 65% sensitivity. For deeply infiltrative disease, specificity was 94% and sensitivity 79%, rising to up to 87% with 3-D ultrasound. For ovarian endometriomas, specificity was 96% and sensitivity 95%. The review regarded positive TVUS findings for ovarian and deep disease as highly certain relative to surgery, but its expert imaging operators may not represent routine practice. Absence of imaging findings cannot establish absence of disease, especially superficial peritoneal disease.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: Use TVUS in the diagnostic assessment, ideally with a sonographer experienced in endometriosis imaging. Consider transabdominal ultrasound when TVUS is unsuitable or intolerable. Negative imaging does not rule out disease, particularly superficial peritoneal disease; persistent symptoms despite negative ultrasound warrant referral for further investigation.

document_sections.heading: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI) Evidence Statement
document_sections.content: According to NICE 2017 and ESHRE 2022, MRI is principally valuable for mapping the presence and extent of deeply infiltrative disease. For rectosigmoid lesions, assessment of invasion depth and length has up to 91% sensitivity and 96% specificity. Reported performance for endometriomas is 91% specificity and 95% sensitivity; performance for superficial peritoneal lesions is limited at 72% specificity and 79% sensitivity. Although MRI and ultrasound appear similar for diagnosis, cost, availability and operator expertise matter. Ultrasound is less expensive and more available, so it is preferred for initial screening.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: TVUS or MRI can contribute to investigation, but negative results cannot exclude endometriosis, especially superficial peritoneal disease. Consider MRI particularly when deep disease is suspected and its extent requires assessment.

document_sections.heading: COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY (CT) AND POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY (PET)
document_sections.content: CT has inadequate pelvic soft-tissue contrast for an appropriate endometriosis diagnostic profile. NICE 2017 and ESHRE 2022 did not evaluate diagnostic CT; the limited evidence cannot establish its comparative performance. CT and PET-CT are not routinely used for diagnosis because supporting evidence is limited relative to ultrasound and MRI; CT access can be limited and radiation exposure unnecessary. CT may nevertheless contribute to surgical planning for deep bladder, ureteric or bowel disease.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: Do not use CT or PET-CT to diagnose endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.3: How reliable are biomarkers for diagnosing endometriosis?
document_sections.content: Reliable diagnostic biomarkers are unavailable. Three Cochrane reviews evaluated endometrial, urinary and blood candidates. Gupta et al. assessed 54 endometrial-biomarker studies, Liu et al. assessed 8 urinary-biomarker studies and Nisenblat et al. assessed 141 blood-biomarker studies; none identified a biomarker able to replace laparoscopy, and many constituent studies had poor methodological quality. A 2016 review of 22 studies reported pooled CA-125 specificity 93% and sensitivity 52%: a positive result may help identify disease, whereas a negative result cannot exclude it. Some evidence suggests better detection of stage III/IV disease.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: Do not use diagnostic biomarkers because of poor positive predictive value, and do not order serum CA-125 for endometriosis diagnosis. If a CA-125 result is obtained incidentally, a value >35 IU/ml may be compatible with endometriosis, while disease remains possible with a value <35 IU/ml.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.4: Is laparoscopy better than empiric medical treatment at managing symptoms in women suspected of having endometriosis?
document_sections.content: Laparoscopy with biopsy has traditionally been considered the diagnostic gold standard, but ESHRE 2022 notes invasiveness, possible surgical morbidity and mortality, expense and regional delays in access. Conversely, photographic and histological confirmation may validate women's experiences and lessen psychological distress. Weigh benefits and risks individually. Offering empirical analgesia and hormonal therapy on a working diagnosis can permit earlier symptom management; the cited rationale is that potential benefit exceeds the generally limited risk of serious adverse events from combined hormonal or progestogen treatment. ESHRE 2022 recommends referral for laparoscopy when suspected disease does not respond to medical therapy, when the woman is attempting conception or when she cannot tolerate treatment. A thorough negative laparoscopy has high specificity and negative predictive value, but incomplete assessment can produce a false-negative result. Histology substantiates visible lesions and can help exclude ovarian malignancy when an endometrioma is drained, sampled or removed; negative histology does not exclude endometriosis. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) system, introduced in 1979 and revised in 1985 as rASRM, is widely used but has observer variability, correlates poorly with pain and does not include deep lesions of the uterosacral ligaments, bladder, vagina or bowel. ENZIAN, introduced in 2005 and revised in 2011, addresses deep and retroperitoneal disease, can be assessed on imaging for surgical planning and tends to correlate with pain, but is not widely used and needs further imaging-based evaluation. The Endometriosis Fertility Index (EFI), introduced in 2010, predicts pregnancy after surgically diagnosed disease. The American Association for Gynaecologic Laparoscopists (AAGL) classification, released in 2021, can use imaging or surgical findings and relates stage to operative complexity, but awaits full validation. With no agreed best classification, a 2017 World Endometriosis Society consensus proposed using rASRM together with ENZIAN for deep disease and EFI for infertility when appropriate.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: For symptoms with suspected endometriosis, empirical medical care and laparoscopy are both reasonable; neither has been shown superior. A suitably trained gynaecologist should systematically inspect the abdomen and pelvis during laparoscopy. Stage disease with the rASRM, EFI and ENZIAN tools where applicable. Biopsy suspicious lesions, recognising that negative histology cannot exclude disease. Discuss the possible treatment and validation benefits of laparoscopy alongside its surgical risks.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.5: What medical management can be offered to women for treatment of endometriosis?
document_sections.content: Select medicines jointly with the woman according to age, symptoms, disease severity, pregnancy intentions, previous treatment, adverse effects and financial burden; one uniform drug choice is unsuitable for every patient.

document_sections.heading: ANALGESIA FOR ENDOMETRIOSIS-ASSOCIATED PAIN Evidence Statement
document_sections.content: The analgesia assessment draws substantially on NICE Clinical Guideline (NG 73) 2017 and ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline 2022.

document_sections.heading: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
document_sections.content: Evidence for NSAIDs and other analgesics in endometriosis largely comes from general pain care rather than disease-specific trials. The NICE 2017 review identified one small crossover RCT of naproxen sodium involving 20 women, conducted in 1985 and judged very low quality. It found no RCTs evaluating other analgesic classes for endometriosis pain, and its search update found no additional studies.

document_sections.heading: Paracetamol
document_sections.content: Paracetamol may be combined with NSAIDs for pain relief but does not change disease pathology. Supporting evidence is very low quality. A review by Zhang et al., based on two relatively small RCTs, found paracetamol no more effective than placebo for pain, whereas co-proxamol (paracetamol 650 mg and dextropropoxyphene 65 mg) reduced pain against placebo. Co-proxamol was withdrawn from the Irish market in 2007 over safety concerns and remains available only on a named-patient basis.

document_sections.heading: Opiate analgesia
document_sections.content: No quality studies evaluate opioids for endometriosis-related pain. Although adding an opioid after inadequate pain control has been discussed, dependency and constipation are concerns in a chronic condition. The NICE committee considered referral for diagnosis potentially more appropriate given other treatment options.

document_sections.heading: Neuromodulator therapies
document_sections.content: Neuromodulators affect central pain mediation and are generally used with a specialist pain service as part of broader care. Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline, selective serotonin uptake inhibitors such as duloxetine, and anticonvulsants such as gabapentin and pregabalin have shown promise. RCTs in chronic pelvic pain, however, have not established clear superiority over placebo, and severe dose-limiting adverse effects sometimes occur. They may be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists and antagonists.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: Paracetamol and NSAIDs, separately or together, may relieve cyclical or menstrual pain; prolonged NSAID use can cause gastrointestinal problems or kidney injury. Analgesics may accompany hormonal suppression for breakthrough pain. Opioids are not recommended for endometriosis-associated pain because of adverse effects and dependence risk. Other analgesics, including neuromodulators, are generally managed with specialist pain input. Refer severe pain unresponsive to first-line analgesia and hormonal suppression to a pain specialist.

document_sections.heading: HORMONAL TREATMENTS FOR ENDOMETRIOSIS-ASSOCIATED PAIN Evidence Statement
document_sections.content: The following evidence concerns hormonal approaches to endometriosis-associated pain, including first-line contraceptive and progestogen treatment and later-line options.

document_sections.heading: Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP)
document_sections.content: Combined hormonal contraceptives are effective first-line treatments for pain. Evidence supporting NICE 2017 recommendations was generally of moderate quality. Three reviews discussed in ESHRE 2022 evaluated the combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP): Grandi et al. reported a statistically significant pain reduction and improved quality of life; another systematic review reported clinically and statistically significant improvements in dysmenorrhea, non-cyclical pelvic pain and dyspareunia; and a Cochrane review found reductions in those symptoms and dyschezia compared with placebo. Available forms are an oral pill, vaginal ring and transdermal patch. In a patient-preference trial, continuous 48-week vaginal-ring treatment with ethinylestradiol (EE) 15 mg + etonogestrel 120 mg/d outperformed a transdermal patch containing EE 20 mg + norelgestromin 150 mg/d. Continuous rather than cyclical COCP use has been suggested for dysmenorrhea. Muzii et al. reported less dysmenorrhea recurrence with continuous treatment (RR 0.24; 95%CI 0.06-0.91). A safety review found no difference in coagulation, metabolism or bone mineral density compared with conventional OCP use.

document_sections.heading: Progestogen therapy
document_sections.content: Progestogens are effective first-line options for endometriosis-related pain and can be delivered as an oral pill, levonorgestrel intra-uterine system (LNGIUS), etonogestrel-releasing subdermal implant or medroxyprogesterone acetate depot intramuscular injection. Acne, oedema, weight gain, irregular bleeding and breast tenderness can limit tolerance. A Cochrane review found similar pain reduction with the evaluated progestogens and anti-progestogens: depot medroxyprogesterone, cyproterone acetate, levonorgestrel, etonogestrel, norethisterone, desogestrel, dienogest and gestrinone. An RCT reported significant visual-analogue pain-score reductions with both an etonogestrel implant and a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system. Danazol is no longer recommended: despite comparable alternatives, its adverse effects include acne, oedema, vaginal bleeding, weight gain, muscle cramps, deeper voice and increased facial hair.

document_sections.heading: Gonadotropin releasing-hormone (GnRH) agonists (e.g. triptorelin, leuprorelin, goserelin) GnRH agonists are effective treatments in reducing endometriosis-associated pain.
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review found GnRH agonists more effective than placebo for pain but less effective than LNG-IUS and oral danazol; effectiveness did not differ across intramuscular, subcutaneous and intranasal delivery. Evidence does not establish a preferred agent, dose or treatment length. Frequently reported adverse effects were vaginal dryness, hot flushes, headache, weight gain and acne; route-comparison studies also reported reduced libido without differences among routes. Prolonged therapy can reduce bone mineral density. Add-back hormone replacement can prevent bone loss; reported regimens include norethisterone/norethindrone acetate (NETA), estrogen-progestin combinations, selective estrogen receptor modulators, bisphosphonates, tibolone and testosterone. A review by Wu et al. of 13 RCTs found moderate-quality support for add-back therapy to prevent bone loss without diminishing agonist effectiveness. A 2023 Cochrane review by Veth et al. found only one suitable trial comparing regimens and remained uncertain about their relative pain effects and adverse events. Across 2 duration trials, pelvic pain might improve more after 6 months than after 3 months, whereas dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia showed opposite results; treatment >6 months was not studied. Across 8 dose trials, pain effects remained uncertain, while higher doses appeared associated with more bone-density loss.

document_sections.heading: Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists (e.g. elagolix, linzagolix, relugolix)
document_sections.content: Two double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs at two elagolix doses found significantly greater pain reduction than placebo. More than 70% of women in each trial group experienced at least one adverse event; event frequency differed significantly between higher-dose elagolix and placebo. Hot flushes, headache and nausea were most frequent. Two smaller RCTs support linzagolix and relugolix efficacy. In the SPIRIT 1 and 2 trials, Giudice et al. evaluated relugolix with add-back 1 mg estradiol and 0.5 mg norethisterone acetate; a delayed arm received 12 weeks of relugolix alone followed by 12 weeks of combination treatment. Dysmenorrhoea improvement versus placebo was SPIRIT 1: 75% versus 27%; SPIRIT 2, 75% versus 30%. Noncyclical pelvic-pain improvement tended to exceed placebo at 59% versus 40%, and 66% versus 43%. After 24 weeks of combination therapy, mean bone-density reduction was less that 1% and was not judged clinically significant. Delaying add-back did not improve efficacy and increased the likelihood of hot flushes and substantial bone-density reduction; the findings suggest combination treatment preserves efficacy while reducing adverse-event risk. A further 80 weeks of extension follow-up was ongoing. Direct comparisons of GnRH agonists and antagonists are scarce. In Ireland, a daily tablet containing 40 mg relugolix/1 mg estradiol hemihydrate/0.5 mg norethisterone is licensed for endometriosis; bone densitometry is recommended after 1 year and subsequently as appropriate, and nonhormonal contraception is required for at least the first month. The National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics Ireland recommended a full Health Technology Assessment; the combination was available but not reimbursed by the HSE when the guideline was published.

document_sections.heading: Aromatase inhibitors (e.g. anastrozole, letrozole)
document_sections.content: RCT evidence of moderate quality indicates reduced pain scores, particularly when other medical or surgical treatments have failed. A 2020 review comprised 15 clinical trials, mostly nonrandomised controlled studies and case reports involving rectovaginal or treatment-refractory disease. Long-term effects are insufficiently studied. Because vaginal dryness, hot flushes and reduced bone mineral density can be severe, reserve these agents until other medical and surgical options are exhausted. They are not currently licensed for endometriosis-related pain. They may be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists and antagonists.

document_sections.heading: Hormonal suppression therapy following surgery for endometriosis
document_sections.content: Postoperative disease and symptom recurrence are substantial: symptoms recur in 40-45% of women, and up to 30% undergo another endometriosis operation within five years of their first. Knez et al. monitored 135 women with moderate or severe deeply infiltrative disease on ultrasound without active treatment for a median 666 days: ultrasound nodules progressed in 37%, regressed in 13% and remained unchanged in 50%. Reviews by Chen et al. and Zakhari et al. suggest postoperative hormonal treatment may reduce recurrence compared with surgery alone when pregnancy is not immediately desired. A separate Knez et al. review found no high-quality evidence for postoperative LNG-IUS to prevent symptomatic recurrence and called for larger studies assessing overall pain, the most troublesome symptom and quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: For suspected disease, clinicians may offer medical treatment without confirmed diagnosis after discussing adverse effects, pregnancy plans and past hormonal-treatment experiences. Goals are to lessen pain frequency and severity, improve quality of life and extend postoperative pain relief. Decide jointly, considering preferences, conception plans, adverse effects, cost and availability. Asymptomatic disease need not be treated. Recommend combined hormonal contraception—oral pill, vaginal ring or patch—or progestogens—oral pill, levonorgestrel intrauterine system, etonogestrel-releasing implant or medroxyprogesterone acetate depot injection—as first-line pain management and to prolong postoperative relief. Recommend continuous combined oral contraception. Reserve GnRH agonists for second line because of adverse effects and uncertainty about dose and duration; prescribe add-back hormones to counter hot flushes, vaginal dryness, bone loss and other treatment-induced menopausal symptoms. Reserve GnRH antagonists for second line because dose and duration lack consensus. Recommend aromatase inhibitors only for pain refractory to other options; they may be combined with oral contraceptives, progestogens or GnRH agonists and antagonists. Postoperative hormonal suppression may reduce recurrent pain.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.6: Is surgery effective for treatment of pain associated with endometriosis?
document_sections.content: Surgery removes lesions by excision, diathermy or ablation and divides adhesions to restore anatomy. Compared with diagnostic laparoscopy alone, operative treatment improves pain scores at six months postoperatively and is associated with better quality of life. A Cochrane review by Bafort et al. considered pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and dyschezia but found insufficient low-quality evidence to identify which pain type responds best.

document_sections.heading: Ablation versus excision for endometriosis
document_sections.content: Pundir et al.'s 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis found excision significantly better than ablation for dyschezia and chronic pelvic-pain scores; lower dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia scores after excision were not statistically significant. A later review by Burks et al. found no significant pain-score difference at 12 months post-operatively. Long-term comparative outcomes are scarce, and reviewed populations included superficial and deep disease, limiting generalisation. The guideline committee favours excision where feasible because tissue can be examined histologically. Ablation's effectiveness for deeply infiltrative disease is unclear, making excision likely more appropriate in that setting.

document_sections.heading: Surgery for endometriomas
document_sections.content: For endometriomas 3 cm or larger, a Cochrane review found both ovarian cystectomy and drainage with bipolar coagulation reduced dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia, but cystectomy with capsule stripping resulted in fewer cyst recurrences, less recurrent non-menstrual pain and fewer repeat operations. A retrospective study (n=125 women) found similar recurrence after cystectomy and laser vaporisation; endometrioma size larger than 5 cm was the leading recurrence risk. Three meta-analyses assessed haemostasis and ovarian reserve after cystectomy: postoperative anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) favoured non-thermal sutures or haemostatic agents over diathermy. Reported ovarian-failure risk after bilateral endometriomata surgery is 2.4%. Drainage with oxidised regenerated cellulose had the smallest AMH effect, whereas combined excision/ablation was associated with lower postoperative ovarian volume than stripping alone. ESHRE 2022 noted that other endometriosis, especially deep disease, is often identified during surgery for painful endometriomas. In a study of 1,191 women undergoing infertility-related ultrasound, 56% (n=70) of those with an endometrioma also had DIE lesions. Preoperative consent should cover general laparoscopic risks, diminished ovarian reserve and possible ovarian loss; for bilateral lesions, discuss possible preoperative oocyte freezing.

document_sections.heading: Surgery for deeply infiltrative endometriosis
document_sections.content: Deeply infiltrative disease extends below the peritoneum and may involve uterosacral ligaments, pelvic sidewalls, rectovaginal septum, vagina, bowel, bladder or ureters. A shared surgical decision requires consent addressing likely outcomes, benefits and risks. Severe disease, especially with bowel involvement, is best managed with multidisciplinary, minimally invasive surgery aiming to remove all lesions. Bowel involvement is reported in 5-12% of women with endometriosis; almost 90% of bowel cases affect sigmoid colon or rectum. Possible symptoms are altered bowel habits, constipation, diarrhoea, tenesmus, dyschezia and rectal bleeding. Colorectal options include superficial shaving, discoid resection and segmental bowel resection. A study of almost 5000 women undergoing laparoscopic rectovaginal excision found significant reductions in premenstrual, menstrual and non-cyclical pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, low-back pain and bladder pain, sustained at two years. Overall complication incidence was 6.8%; major gastrointestinal complications affected 1.1% of operations and urinary-tract complications 1% of procedures. Postoperative complications after bowel surgery have been reported at up to 13.9%, commonly abdominal-wall abscess, voiding dysfunction, urinary-tract infection or unexplained fever. Bladder lesions are usually excised with primary bladder-wall closure. Ureteric lesions may be excised after stenting; intrinsic lesions or marked obstruction may require segmental removal with end-to-end anastomosis or reimplantation. In a review of 700 women, ureteric disease usually lacked specific urinary symptoms; the left ureter was affected in 53.6%, bilateral disease occurred in 10.6% of cases and concurrent bladder involvement in 19.8% of patients. Ureterolysis alone was performed in 579 patients, ureteral resection and re-anastomosis in 89 patients, and ureteroneocystostomy in 32.

document_sections.heading: Hysterectomy for treatment of endometriosis
document_sections.content: No RCTs assess hysterectomy for endometriosis pain, although other evidence associates hysterectomy with or without oophorectomy with substantial pain reduction. Martin's narrative review found benefit for many women with associated chronic nonspecific pelvic pain, but some experienced no relief; retaining ovaries increased the risk of recurrent pain and further surgery. Reported risks after hysterectomy with ovarian conservation were 6-fold for recurrent pain and 8.1-times greater for reoperation; these must be weighed against hormone-replacement needs and potential long-term effects of oophorectomy. Evidence on menopausal hormonal therapy (MHT) after surgical menopause is sparse. A review restricted to two RCTs found a small association with disease recurrence, supporting continuous oestrogen-progestogen MHT when it is needed after endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content:
Offer surgery as one option for endometriosis-associated pain. Before surgery, discuss the procedure, expected effect on symptoms, risks, benefits and possible need for another operation. Use laparoscopy rather than laparotomy unless contraindicated, and consider excision instead of ablation for pain. For endometrioma, consider ovarian cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage with coagulation to reduce recurrence and pain. Minimise ovarian injury, particularly with recurrent endometrioma or concern about ovarian reserve.

For women who no longer intend to conceive and have not benefited from conservative treatment, hysterectomy with or without ovarian removal may be considered. If hysterectomy is chosen, the guideline favours total over sub-total hysterectomy because endometriosis may persist in or near a retained cervix. All visible lesions should be excised during hysterectomy. Women should understand that hysterectomy does not necessarily eliminate symptoms. If a woman with previous endometriosis needs menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen is advised.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: 19. Offer surgery as an option for reducing endometriosis-associated pain (Grade 1A). 20. Choose hormonal or surgical pain treatment jointly with the woman, accounting for her preferences, adverse effects, individual treatment effectiveness, cost and availability (Best practice). 21. If operating, clinicians may favour excision over ablation for endometriosis-associated pain (Grade 2A). 22. During surgery for a painful endometrioma, anticipate other endometriosis, including deeply infiltrative endometriosis, because it is commonly present (Best practice). 23. For ovarian endometrioma, perform cystectomy or CO2 laser vaporisation rather than drainage and coagulation to reduce recurrence of the endometrioma and associated pain; minimise ovarian injury (Grade 1B). 24. Excision of deeply infiltrative endometriosis may lessen associated pain and improve quality of life (Grade 1B). 25. An experienced deep-disease surgeon should undertake that excision, preferably with a multidisciplinary team using a minimally invasive approach intended to remove all lesions (Best practice). 26. Consider hysterectomy, with or without oophorectomy, when conservative care has failed and pregnancy is not planned; explain that symptoms may remain (Grade 2B). 27. Perform total rather than sub-total hysterectomy (Best practice). 28. Before considering oophorectomy, discuss early menopause and the potential need for MHT (Grade 1B). 29. When MHT is needed after endometriosis, use a continuous oestrogen-progestogen regimen (Grade 1C).

document_sections.heading: Section 3: Treatment of endometriosis-associated infertility
document_sections.content: This section considers medical treatment, surgery and fertility treatments for infertility associated with endometriosis.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.7: What management is recommended for endometriosis-associated infertility?
document_sections.content: Endometriosis and infertility frequently occur together; endometriosis is present in 35-50% of women presenting with infertility. Infertility can be the initial complaint whether or not pain is present. Hormonal treatments for endometriosis interfere with ovulation, so they are unsuitable while attempting conception; this complicates pain care and often leads to early fertility referral. Because endometriosis is an established infertility risk factor, referral is advised sooner than for women of the same age without known risk factors. Evidence for managing this infertility is scarce, especially for live birth outcomes. The guideline directs readers seeking further fertility guidance to the 2023 National Clinical Practice Guideline: Fertility – Investigation and Management in Secondary Care.

document_sections.heading: Medical management
document_sections.content: In a 2007 Cochrane review, Hughes et al. found no benefit in clinical pregnancy rates from ovarian suppression compared with placebo in women with endometriosis; live birth data were lacking. A 2020 Cochrane review suggested that hormonal treatment after endometriosis surgery increased the chance of pregnancy from 34% to 35-48%. That analysis combined spontaneous and assisted pregnancies and did not give total time to pregnancy. It suggested no harm to future fertility from postoperative hormonal therapy; this treatment should be considered if conception cannot be attempted immediately, because it improves pain.

document_sections.heading: Surgical management Stage I-II endometriosis
document_sections.content: The effect of surgery on spontaneous conception may vary with disease stage or type. A 2020 Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence that surgery for stage I-II endometriosis improves the likelihood of a viable intrauterine pregnancy compared with diagnostic laparoscopy alone, but live birth data were unavailable. Another meta-analysis reported more pregnancies after operative laparoscopy.

document_sections.heading: Ovarian and tubal endometriosis
document_sections.content: Randomised trials comparing surgery with conservative management for infertility associated with ovarian endometriosis are lacking. Surgical approaches include cystectomy and coagulation of the cyst lining. Candiani et al. reported postoperative pregnancy rates of 72.2% after cystectomy and 74.3% after CO2 laser cyst vaporisation in 2021; spontaneous pregnancy was more frequent after cystectomy (55.5% vs 35.9%). Surgery for recurrent or bilateral endometriomas needs particular caution because cystectomy can be especially harmful to ovarian reserve. In a meta-analysis of eight studies, Alshehre et al. found fewer retrieved oocytes in women with endometriomas but no other reproductive-outcome differences during IVF or ICSI. Evidence increasingly supports removing an endometrioma only when it causes pain or obstructs ovarian access for oocyte retrieval. ESHRE advises against routine endometrioma surgery before ART, while allowing consideration for pain or follicular access. Muzii et al. suggested observation for asymptomatic endometriomas but noted concern that untreated cysts might reduce ovarian reserve; they proposed serial assessment of cyst size and ovarian-reserve markers, AMH or antral follicle count. In a 2020 Cochrane review of 11 RCTs, Melo et al. found moderate-quality evidence that salpingectomy before ART probably increases pregnancy rates in tubal disease. Tubal occlusion may also increase pregnancy rates, although supporting evidence is low quality.

document_sections.heading: Deeply infiltrative endometriosis
document_sections.content: Evidence about pregnancy after surgery for deeply infiltrative endometriosis (DIE) is limited. In a review of 49 studies, only 37% reported pregnancy rates; reported rates were 23-57%, and cumulative rates within four years were 58-70%. Active intention to conceive, time to conception and spontaneous versus assisted conception were often unspecified. Cohen et al. reported a postoperative spontaneous pregnancy rate of 50.5% for DIE without bowel involvement, rising to 68.3% when assisted pregnancies were included; rates before or without surgery were unavailable. For bowel involvement, postoperative spontaneous and overall pregnancy rates were 28.6% and 46.9%, respectively, compared with 29% after ART without surgery. Another review found no randomised trials and considered the data too poor for firm conclusions; spontaneous postoperative pregnancy was 49% across 4 retrospective studies and 21% across 3 prospective studies. A 2012 review by Vercellini et al. reported 39% conception overall after surgery and 24% among women with infertility seeking spontaneous conception. Because evidence that DIE excision before ART improves reproductive outcomes is sparse, ESHRE bases that decision on pain and the woman's preference.

document_sections.heading: Intrauterine Insemination (IUI)
document_sections.content: Randomised trials provide some evidence that, for stage I-II endometriosis, IUI with ovarian stimulation produces more live births than expectant care and more biochemical pregnancies than IUI without stimulation. During the six months after stage I/II surgery, clinical pregnancy rates with stimulated IUI resemble those in unexplained infertility. For stage III-IV disease, only retrospective evidence suggests a higher ongoing pregnancy rate after six stimulated IUI cycles.

document_sections.heading: Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)
document_sections.content: Here ART means interventions that handle embryos or oocytes. No randomised trial compares ART with expectant care in women with endometriosis, so outcome evidence is indirect and findings about endometriosis are conflicting. A meta-analysis found no significant overall difference in clinical pregnancy or live birth versus women without endometriosis, but found lower clinical pregnancy and a trend toward fewer live births in stage III-IV disease. A large USA retrospective cohort found a 24% lower live birth rate on the first treatment cycle than in unexplained infertility, with a more marked effect at higher stages. A population-based USA retrospective study of 347,185 ART cycles found lower live birth rates than in unexplained or tubal infertility: endometriosis combined with other diagnoses had the lowest chance, whereas isolated endometriosis had rates similar to other diagnoses. Another retrospective study of 27,294 ART cycles found fewer oocytes and more cancellations with endometriosis, without lower pregnancy or live birth rates. A review of endometriomata found fewer retrieved and mature oocytes but no evidence of lower implantation, clinical pregnancy or live birth rates. The Endometriosis Fertility Index (EFI) predicts natural or IUI conception after surgery using age, previous pregnancy and surgical factors. A meta-analysis of over 30 studies validated its good performance despite study heterogeneity. The EFI may inform assessment before surgery of the prospect of spontaneous pregnancy afterward and help identify women who might benefit from ART.

document_sections.heading: Investigation/workup
document_sections.content: Assess disease stage and whether involvement is peritoneal, ovarian and/or deeply infiltrative. Also evaluate the woman or couple's fertility factors, including ovarian reserve and semen analysis. Involvement of the fertility team is advised to tailor care.

document_sections.heading: Medical treatment
document_sections.content: Women may have pain, difficulty conceiving or both. Hormonal pain treatment suppresses ovulation and is therefore unsuitable during attempts to conceive. Ovarian suppression or other hormone therapy can be considered after surgery when pregnancy is not immediately desired or possible: it improves surgical pain outcomes without adversely affecting later fertility.

document_sections.heading: Surgical treatment
document_sections.content: Decisions about surgery should reflect pain, previous operations and the woman's preference. Shared decision-making should include other fertility results, including her partner's semen analysis. Recurrent or bilateral endometrioma warrants particular caution because of the possible effect of surgery on ovarian reserve.

document_sections.heading: Intrauterine insemination (IUI)
document_sections.content: Where available, IUI may be considered for stage I-II disease and may work particularly well within six months after surgery. For stage III-IV disease with confirmed patent tubes, IUI could be considered, but evidence is limited.

document_sections.heading: Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)
document_sections.content: ART, including in vitro fertilisation and ICSI, can treat infertility associated with endometriosis; similar clinical outcomes to controls suggest potential benefit. Surgery before ART may be needed for hydrosalpinx, DIE or ovaries inaccessible for oocyte retrieval.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: 30. Do not prescribe hormonal suppression to women with endometriosis-associated infertility who are trying to conceive (Grade 1A). 31. When contemplating infertility surgery, consider age, ovarian reserve, duration of infertility and other fertility factors (Best practice). 32. Offer operative laparoscopy for infertility with stage I-II endometriosis because it improves the chance of an ongoing clinical pregnancy (Grade 1A). 33. For infertility with endometrioma, operative laparoscopy may be considered to improve spontaneous pregnancy prospects; decide jointly, accounting for ovarian reserve, earlier surgery, symptoms, other fertility investigations and planned fertility treatment (Grade 1A). 34. Do not routinely operate on an endometrioma before ART; surgery may be considered for pain or access to follicles (Best practice). 35. Consider operative laparoscopy as an option for women with symptomatic deeply infiltrative endometriosis and infertility, guided by pain and their preference (Grade 2B). 36. Consider IUI with ovarian stimulation for infertility with stage I-II endometriosis (Grade 2B). 37. Use ART for endometriosis-associated infertility, particularly with impaired tubal function or coexisting male-factor infertility (Grade 1C).

document_sections.heading: Section 4: Role of non-medical interventions for the treatment of endometriosis
document_sections.content: This section examines non-medical strategies for symptoms, quality of life and psychological well-being.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2.8: What is the role of non-medical interventions in the management of endometriosis?
document_sections.content: In a study by Schwartz et al., 62.5% of women with endometriosis in Switzerland, Austria and Germany used complementary and alternative medicine. An Australian survey by Armour et al. found that at least 70% used self-management, including heat, dietary measures, meditation, breathing exercises, non-prescribed drugs and alcohol. Self-management enables active participation in care and has been associated with greater knowledge and self-efficacy. Drawing on European Association of Urology chronic-pelvic-pain guidance, a multidisciplinary approach is strongly recommended for gynaecological aspects of that pain. Even if pain cannot be improved, women should have options addressing psychological, sexual and physical contributors to quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Acupuncture
document_sections.content: A 2011 Cochrane review identified only 1 eligible RCT, comparing acupuncture with Chinese herbs in 67 women. Severe dysmenorrhoea decreased significantly with acupuncture, but mild-to-moderate dysmenorrhoea did not differ; the review could not recommend acupuncture and called for larger trials. A 2016 meta-analysis of 3 studies involving 99 women suggested it could be tried as a generally safe adjunct. A 2017 review of 1 RCT and 9 small Chinese studies found consistent support for relief of dysmenorrhoea and pain but could not analyse quality of life. Because studies are small, nonspecific and unblinded, acupuncture may be considered alongside other treatment, but no recommendation can be made for endometriosis-associated pain or quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Physical therapies
document_sections.content: Little research addresses physiotherapy specifically in endometriosis, so the committee also drew on pelvic-floor dysfunction and general pelvic-pain evidence. Physiotherapy approaches vary and may address activity through exercise, pacing and goals, identify fears or beliefs, and incorporate behavioural approaches to persistent pain. A 2012 review of six RCTs in chronic pelvic pain found the available studies small and mostly non-randomised; specific recommendations need caution. Because treatments differed and were combined with psychological and medical care, physiotherapy's independent effect could not be determined. A 2019 review found 2 eligible trigger-point manual-therapy trials; they showed no significant pain reduction against general massage and did not support recommending trigger-point therapy for chronic pain.

document_sections.heading: Electrotherapy
document_sections.content: Three small studies examined electrotherapy for endometriosis-associated pain; the author subsequently retracted the Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) study. In a retrospective study by Bi et al. of 83 treated women, neuromuscular electrical stimulation produced no initial improvement at 5 weeks, but pain differed statistically significantly at 10 weeks compared with 71 untreated women. In a small RCT by Thabet et al., 2 groups of 20 women received high-intensity or sham laser therapy, both with hormonal treatment. After 8 weeks, 85% of the active-treatment group reported significant improvement in pain and quality of life. Study designs and small samples prevent a recommendation about electrotherapy for pain or quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Psychological interventions
document_sections.content: Clinicians should recognise the psychological effects of chronic pain and infertility. Although more studies examine psychological interventions, overlapping outcomes such as pain, quality of life, infertility, anxiety and depression make intervention effects difficult to separate. In a 2017 narrative review, Buggio et al. proposed that individual or group support-expressive psychotherapy might benefit women and called for properly designed trials to establish benefit. A 2019 review of 11 studies by Van Niekerk et al. judged study quality weak, bias risk high and effectiveness findings inconclusive. A 2019 review of 12 studies by Evans et al. reached similar conclusions while finding the pilot results promising for pain, anxiety, depression, stress and fatigue. Better-designed studies are needed before effectiveness recommendations can be made.

document_sections.heading: Nutrition
document_sections.content: A dietary effect on symptoms through inflammation, prostaglandin metabolism and oestrogen activity remains speculative. Dietary changes may enable women to participate in managing their condition and might improve quality of life, but studies of symptom benefit are very limited. Women with endometriosis have higher reported prevalences of food intolerance (25.6% vs 7.7%), allergies (57% vs 31%) and gastrointestinal symptoms (77% vs 29%). A 2013 review of 12 trials, including 3 animal studies, found a relatively strong association with trans-fatty-acid consumption and lower endometriosis and pain risk with omega-3-rich diets; results for vegetables, fibre and fruit were equivocal. A 2020 review of 12 studies, all of low to very low quality, suggested fatty acids, antioxidants and certain vitamins and minerals might improve symptoms. In a qualitative study of n=12, women making individual dietary changes described less pain and fatigue, greater well-being and improved understanding of their bodies.

document_sections.heading: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)
document_sections.content: Evidence for TCM in endometriosis symptoms is scarce. The ESHRE review judged available studies insufficiently robust and generally poorly designed, so it could not recommend TCM for improving quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Nurse Specialists
document_sections.content: The endometriosis role of clinical nurse specialists (CNS) is relatively new and still developing. Within multidisciplinary teams, they connect women with specialist services and support patient-centred care. Research is needed into the costs and benefits of CNS-led activities, including clinics.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: Clinicians should acknowledge the psychological burden of endometriosis, whose aetiology and prognosis are uncertain and whose consequences can include disabling pain and subfertility requiring long-term support. They should be prepared to discuss non-medical options for quality of life and psychological well-being, including local support groups. Although the Endometriosis Clinical Nurse Specialist role continues to develop, it contributes importantly to woman-centred multidisciplinary care.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: 38. No recommendation can be made for any individual non-medical intervention—traditional Chinese medicine, nutrition, electrotherapy, acupuncture, physiotherapy or psychological interventions—to treat endometriosis-related symptoms. Clinicians may nevertheless discuss these approaches with women in relation to quality of life and psychological well-being (Best practice).

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Literature search strategy
document_sections.content: The developers reviewed national and international publications. Their reference guidelines were the ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline 2022 and NICE Clinical Guideline (NG 73) 2017. Searches of Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews covered newer evidence through June 2023 and used broad and focused endometriosis-treatment terms. Recommendations considered the available evidence as a whole and adopted or adapted ESHRE recommendations. Publication date was considered without a fixed limit; guidance from other professional organisations was also examined.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Appraisal of evidence
document_sections.content: Developers appraised study design, the relevance of primary and secondary outcomes, consistency between studies, the balance of benefit and harm, and applicability to practice. Agreed evidence-based recommendations were adapted where necessary for Irish care.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 AGREE II process
document_sections.content: During development, the guideline was assessed with the AGREE II checklist. AGREE II provides a framework for evaluating guideline quality, guiding development methods and specifying what guideline reports should contain.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Literature review
document_sections.content: Four reviewers assessed the selected literature alongside the ESHRE evidence base, and two reviewers evaluated evidence quality using GRADE. The development group identified low-quality evidence or an absence of evidence in many areas of endometriosis diagnosis, management and care, while considering many recommendations applicable in Ireland. Adaptations for the Irish setting were identified.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Grades of recommendation
document_sections.content: GRADE structures evidence summaries and recommendation development. The developers state that an extensive GRADE assessment was not feasible for this work, but they used the suggested recommendation language in the GRADE table.

document_sections.heading: 3.6 Future research
document_sections.content: The guideline identifies evidence gaps and cites research priorities concerning a cure and causes of endometriosis; education that shortens diagnostic delay and improves care; non-invasive screening and improved diagnosis; preservation or maximisation of fertility; management of emotional, psychological and fatigue effects; outcomes of treatments intended to treat or cure disease rather than only manage it; prevention of progression or spread; and the most effective non-surgical symptom and pain treatments. Additional proposed questions concern how long effective GnRH agonist treatment can safely continue; the effects of GnRH antagonists and aromatase inhibitors on quality of life and pain; and whether dietary changes, psychological interventions or physical therapies improve those outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Education plans required to implement the Guideline
document_sections.content: Implementation should be accompanied by continuing local and national education, training and assessment. Units providing endometriosis surgery ultimately need to audit surgeon training, continuing competence and outcomes. The guideline describes plans for surgical training, specialist-trainee education and prioritisation of advanced endometriosis fellowships, particularly for complex cases. It also calls for menstrual-health education for girls and young women, more proactive questions about symptoms such as dysmenorrhoea, and accessible, high-quality educational resources.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Barriers and facilitators
document_sections.content: Potential implementation barriers include budgets and service redesign, facilities and equipment, professional knowledge and training, and patients' perceptions. Referral to surgeons capable of assessing and biopsying suspected lesions requires suitable training and workforce planning. The guideline calls for dedicated endometriosis clinical leadership and recognition of symptoms at first healthcare contact to shorten diagnostic delay. Geography and population density may limit equitable access to specialist gynaecologists. Multidisciplinary specialist centres may improve outcomes, but access to them can appear unequal. Telemedicine could improve consultations but is unlikely to replace the in-person diagnosis and treatment usually needed. Smaller centres can provide initial assessment and conservative treatment, with referral or follow-up at larger tertiary centres.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Resources necessary to implement recommendations
document_sections.content: Historically, endometriosis care through general gynaecology services in Ireland has varied in availability and practice, with long waits and cost pressures. The National Framework for Endometriosis Care provides for additional multidisciplinary staff and two Supra-regional centres intended specifically for women with Stage 4 endometriosis. Hospitals should compare current services with the guideline and identify resource gaps. Full implementation, including surgery at every level, requires appropriate facilities, expertise and multidisciplinary care. The guideline also proposes online learning resources and tools to improve awareness, detection and management.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Introduction to audit
document_sections.content: Institutions and professionals are encouraged to audit both implementation and effects on women's outcomes regularly, identifying responsible personnel when a new guideline version is received.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Auditable standards
document_sections.content: Units should track information systematically, use key recommendations to identify improvements and compare audit results with other endometriosis services. Proposed measures cover: 1. the proportion of symptomatic women offered appropriate abdominal and pelvic examination; 2. numbers receiving a working diagnosis at first presentation; 3. time from first presentation to diagnosis; 4. the proportion whose initial hormonal treatment is ineffective after six months, intolerable or contraindicated, alongside evidence of referral pathways; 5. the proportion referred to gynaecology who undergo laparoscopy; 6. referral-to-laparoscopy time; 7. linkage with an Endometriosis Nurse Specialist; 8. referral for pelvic physiotherapy; 9. referral to a Pain Specialist; 10. referral to a Psychologist; 11. referral to a Dietician; 12. receipt of transvaginal ultrasound during initial investigation; 13. referral for fertility advice; 14. specialist-centre referral for suspected or confirmed bowel, bladder or ureter deeply infiltrative endometriosis, with local referral protocols; 15. diagnosis rates for disease involving those organs; 16. surgical-treatment rates for such disease; 17. histological confirmation after biopsy or excision in women with suspected disease; 18. surgical complications and readmissions after operations involving bowel, bladder or ureter disease; 19. patient-reported satisfaction with surgery; and 20. re-operation within 5 years of endometriosis surgery. The results are intended to inform local care pathways, staffing and service planning.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Evaluation
document_sections.content: Evaluation assesses whether an intervention achieved its intended outcomes. Guideline implementation will undergo periodic national audit against standards set by NWIHP; senior hospital clinical management should also evaluate the auditable standards locally.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Procedure for the update of the Guideline
document_sections.content: New evidence may require revision. National review is planned every three years, or sooner when circumstances warrant, with literature and recent evidence assessed to decide on changes. Even when no amendment is needed, the revision record requires a new version number and date. Existing recommendations remain valid until review is completed.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Method for amending the Guideline
document_sections.content: Guidelines require updating as new evidence becomes available. Review can be requested when 3 years have elapsed since publication, 3 years have elapsed since the last review, or new evidence requires an update. Requests should be handled promptly.

document_sections.heading: Appendix 4: GRADE Table
document_sections.content: The table explains how recommendation grades relate to the balance of benefit and harm, evidence quality, clinical implications and suggested wording. Grade 1A denotes a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence; 1B, a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence; and 1C, a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. Grade 2A denotes a weak recommendation with high-quality evidence; 2B, a weak recommendation with moderate-quality evidence; and 2C, a weak recommendation with low-quality evidence. For weak grades, the preferable action may vary with circumstances or values; for 2C, alternatives may be equally reasonable. Best practice identifies a recommendation for which desirable effects are considered to outweigh undesirable effects despite the absence of direct evidence, making evidence grading unnecessary.
